q: State the weather rhythm noble rot requires, and the single change that turns it into grey rot.
accept: misty mornings then dry sunny afternoons continuous wet gives grey rot
humid mornings dry afternoons in alternation rain with no drying gives grey rot
fog then sun and it turns grey when it never dries
ans: Alternation. Humid, misty mornings — typically river or lake fog — let Botrytis cinerea infect ripe, intact fruit; dry, breezy, sunny afternoons then dehydrate the berry and check the fungus, concentrating sugar and acid and building the glycerol and botrytis aromatics. Remove the drying window — continuous wet weather — or let the rot arrive on unripe or damaged fruit, and you get grey rot: acetic and mould spoilage, laccase, colour and fruit destroyed.
exp: The geography follows from the mechanism: the cold Ciron meeting the warmer Garonne at Sauternes, the shallow Neusiedlersee at Rust, the Layon's tributary fogs, the Mosel and Rhine's morning mists. Two winemaking consequences worth carrying: botrytised must arrives loaded with laccase, an oxidative enzyme far more aggressive than the grape's own tyrosinase, so handling and SO2 discipline are critical; and successive tries through the vineyard are not romance but necessity, because the fungus never advances evenly.

q: Downy and powdery mildew differ in pathogen, in what they need to spread, and in the classic treatment. Give all three.
accept: downy plasmopara needs rain treated with copper powdery erysiphe needs humidity treated with sulfur
downy oomycete rain copper bordeaux mixture powdery fungus humidity sulfur
copper for downy sulfur for powdery
plasmopara viticola copper erysiphe necator sulfur
downy needs free water powdery only needs humidity
ans: Downy mildew (Plasmopara viticola) is an oomycete needing warm rain and free water — oil spots above the leaf, white 'down' beneath — treated with copper (Bordeaux mixture); powdery mildew (Erysiphe necator) is a true fungus needing only humidity, dusty grey growth on the surface, treated with sulfur
exp: Both are American imports, but they arrived a generation apart: powdery mildew (oïdium) reached England in 1845 and had swept France by the early 1850s, where sulfur dusting became the answer, while downy mildew followed around 1878 and Millardet published Bordeaux mixture — copper sulfate and lime — in 1885. The divide is the whole spray calendar: copper against downy, sulfur against powdery. The distinction that catches candidates is water — downy cannot infect without free water on the leaf, powdery only wants humid air, so a dry warm summer suppresses one and encourages the other. Copper's persistence in soil is why organic rules cap it (the EU renewal limits copper to 28 kg/ha averaged over seven years), which is the pressure driving PIWI plantings.

exp: Oriental replaced 'Baja'; the reforms added viñedos singulares, vinos de zona and municipio.

q: Explain why Champagne pairs with fried food at a molecular level.
accept: acidity cuts fat co2 scrubs palate autolytic notes echo maillard
ans: Acid cuts fat, CO2 physically scrubs the palate, and autolytic bread-toast notes echo the Maillard browning of the crust
exp: Three mechanisms in one glass — the reason it is the somm's cheat code.

q: Sommelier's order of introduction when presenting a bottle to a mixed-language table:
accept: producer wine appellation vintage clearly host language courtesy
label facing host announce producer cuvee appellation vintage
ans: Label to the host; announce producer, cuvée, appellation, vintage — clearly, once, in the table's language of comfort
exp: Precision and warmth in one breath; never quiz the guest.
